legal.headline: Indian courts can modify rather than quash awards to avoid hardship and delay, Supreme Court clarifies
legal.hook: Indian courts can modify rather than quash awards to avoid hardship and delay, Supreme Court clarifies CDR News
legal.summary: The Supreme Court of India has clarified that Indian courts possess the authority to modify arbitral awards rather than outright quashing them, a stance intended to reduce unnecessary hardship and prevent procedural delays. This clarification addresses the interpretation of judicial powers under India's arbitration framework, specifically regarding the grounds on which courts can intervene in awards. By permitting modification as an alternative to quashing, the Court aims to balance the finality of arbitration with the need for corrective intervention when awards contain errors or issues that warrant adjustment. The judgment suggests courts should consider less drastic remedies before resorting to complete nullification of awards. This approach seeks to streamline dispute resolution and reduce the litigation burden caused by protracted quashing petitions that ultimately require re-arbitration. The decision has implications for how courts exercise their supervisory jurisdiction over arbitral proceedings.
legal.contextNote: Under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Section 34 permits courts to set aside arbitral awards on specific grounds (procedural irregularity, jurisdiction issues, public policy violation). However, the distinction between modification and quashing has remained ambiguous in practice, leading to inconsistent application across High Courts. This Supreme Court clarification is significant for practitioners advising on post-award remedies, as it expands judicial discretion and potentially reduces the finality doctrine's rigidity. The ruling impacts commercial arbitration across sectors (infrastructure, M&A, corporate disputes) and affects cost-benefit calculations for challenging awards. Indian lawyers should revise challenge strategies: modification may now be preferred where full quashing seems disproportionate. This also influences how arbitrators draft awards to anticipate modification risks. business.hook: Indian banks’ RoA is expected to ease to 1.15–1.2% this fiscal from 1.3% last year, driven by lower treasury income and higher pre-emptive provisioning ahead of the ECL framework.
business.summary: Indian banks' Return on Assets (RoA) is projected to decline by 10–15 basis points to 1.15–1.2% in the current fiscal year from 1.3% in the previous year, according to CRISIL's assessment. The contraction is attributed to two primary factors: lower treasury income and higher pre-emptive provisioning ahead of the implementation of the Expected Credit Loss (ECL) framework. Despite this decline, the report indicates that net interest margins remain stable and asset quality risks are contained. CRISIL's analysis suggests that while profitability will face headwinds, the overall resilience of Indian banks' profitability should be maintained through the fiscal year, even as they navigate the operational and balance-sheet adjustments necessitated by regulatory changes.

This affects Ind AS compliance and balance-sheet provisioning under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
